voyage.name: Cenotaph
voyage.content: Built in 1923 in honour of the fallen soldiers of World War I and later also attributed to the ones from World War II. It is a copy of the more famous one in London. There is a ceremony on on the second Sunday of November to commemorate the fallen soldiers.

voyage.name: City Hall
voyage.content: Concert hall, theatre, and exhibition space. This cultural hub is famous for its dim sum restaurant.

voyage.name: Government House
voyage.content: Originally the official residence of the British Governors of Hong Kong under colonial rule, since the handover back to China in 1997, it has been the official residence of the Chief Executive of Hong Kong. Only open to the public on specific open days that are usually published on the web-site in advance, usually once in the spring to coincide with the blooming of the flowers in the garden, and once in the autumn.

voyage.name: Man Mo Temple Compound
voyage.content: Consists of Man Mo Temple, Lit Shing Kung Temple and Kung Sor assembly hall. Man Mo Temple was built in the 1840s and is Hong Kong Island's oldest temple. It is nestled amongst antique shops, with the air full of smoke from hundreds of burning incense coils. While you are there, pop into one of the many antique shops to see some of the best Chinese and South-East Asian antiques in the world, and the many very clever

voyage.name: Statue Square
voyage.content: Public square built in the 19th century with a number of royal statues. Now the only statue is of banker Sir Thomas Jackson. It is a relaxing place with plantings and fountains. The square is surrounded by some impressive buildings, including the HSBC headquarters and the Legislative Council.

voyage.name: Jamia Mosque
voyage.content: Constructed in 1890, it is the oldest mosque in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Ohel Leah Synagogue
voyage.content: Orthodox synagogue built by Baghdadi Jews in 1902. Most of Hong Kong's Jewish community lives in the surrounding neighbourhood.

voyage.name: Dr Sun Yat-sen Museum
voyage.content: Exhibits on the life of Sun Yat-sen.

voyage.name: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
voyage.content: Museum of teapots and cups, with exhibits ranging from modern to 3000 years old.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences
voyage.content: The neighbour of one of the earliest hospitals in Hong Kong, Tung Wah Hospital, this museum shows how the healthcare system evolved from traditional Chinese medicine to modern Western medicine, via the establishment of numerous hospitals and the first medical school (now the University of Hong Kong), of which Dr. Sun Yat-sen was a student.

voyage.name: City Gallery
voyage.content: A celebration of planning proposals and infrastructure projects. Interactive features and devices give visitors the latest information on planning and infrastructure developments in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Visual Arts Centre
voyage.content: Offers visual arts studios for artists as well as exhibition halls.

voyage.name: Madame Tussaud's
voyage.content: The usual Tussaud's waxworks with characters that appeal to Chinese interests.

voyage.name: University Museum and Art Gallery
voyage.content: The oldest museum in Hong Kong dating back to 1953 has a large permanent collection of Chinese antiquities as well as modern paintings. It also host exhibitions of contemporary and ancient art.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Maritime Museum
voyage.price: $30, half price for seniors and students
voyage.content: In addition to original artifacts, cannons, scrolls, ship's models and paintings, the galleries of Hong Kong Maritime Museum have over 25 interactive screens using the latest technology to introduce visitors to the vast range of stories and topics at the heart of Hong Kong's – and the world's – maritime story. You can learn of Poon Lim, the world record holder for solo survival at sea. See how a junk is built. Trace

voyage.name: Trick Eye Museum Hong Kong
voyage.address: Level 3, The Peak Galleria, 118 Peak Road, The Peak
voyage.content: The only Korean 3D museum in Hong Kong. It presents a magnificent collection of 3D art pieces. It features paintings on plain surfaces that magically appear to be three dimensional through the use of optical illusion. You are most welcome to touch, climb and interact with the amazing exhibits. You can also enjoy the free observation deck view of the beautiful Harbour View.

voyage.name: Chater Garden
voyage.content: Adjacent to the Legislative Council Building, this is the place where disgruntled Hongkongers come to protest. Named after businessman Sir Paul Chater.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Park
voyage.content: A great place to relax in Central. Head for L16 cafe and bar which is one of the few places where you can eat and drink outdoors away from the traffic.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens
voyage.content: A small, free zoo with reptiles, primates, a jaguar, and rare and endangered birds and plants.

voyage.name: Lung Fu Shan Country Park
voyage.content: Hong Kong newest and smallest Country Park. Its proximity to the Peak makes it highly accessible and one is rewarded by a pleasant hike away from the crowds nearby. A convenient place to make a BBQ with great views over Victoria Harbour. Budding military historians will enjoy exploring Pinewood battery and other remnants of the Second World War.

voyage.name: Central-Mid-Levels Escalator
voyage.content: At 800 m long, this is the longest outdoor covered escalator system in the world. The escalator runs downhill from 6AM to 10AM and uphill from 10:30AM to midnight every day. Part of it near the bottom goes along Cochrane Street, and it's hard to miss. It goes from busy areas at the bottom to upscale residential neighborhoods at the top. voyage.name: Mount Davis
voyage.content: Walk up Mount Davis to see the abandoned Second World War-era gunnery fortifications. Take the steps up from Victoria Rd just west of Kennedy Town; or follow Victoria Rd until you reach the roundabout (about a kilometre), and take the mountain road up. voyage.name: Sheung Wan Civic Centre
voyage.address: 5/F., Sheung Wan Municipal Services Building, 345 Queen's Road Central,
voyage.content: Theatre and concert venue.

voyage.name: Wellington St
voyage.content: Nice street with dried foodstuffs, various restaurants, majong pieces. Also check out Art Jam at 123 Wellington St. They provide you with canvas, paints and materials. From $200 to $500 depending on when you go and canvas size.

voyage.name: Yan Shang Kee
voyage.content: Rent a qipao to wear for a day while exploring Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Flow
voyage.content: Second-hand bookshop where you can exchange your used travel guides.

voyage.name: Hollywood Road
voyage.content: Antiques.

voyage.name: IFC Mall

Here you will find one of the best cinemas with the added bonus that the film will be the English language version (if it is an animation). Go up to the rooftop and you will find yourself in public open space. The views of Victoria Harbour are good and you will find a couple of bars that will help you enjoy the public terrace on

voyage.name: The Landmark
voyage.content: An older shopping centre that has had a facelift to incorporate a five-star hotel. For many, it remains a focus for many of the most expensive designer fashion shops in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Pedder St and Queen's Rd
voyage.content: One of the best locations for jewellery and designer watches at prices that can be up to 35% less than Europe. As always, shop around for the best prices and always buy from reputable dealers to avoid fake goods.

voyage.name: Pacific Place and Queensway and Admiralty Centre
voyage.content: A number of interconnected shopping malls connected to Admiralty MTR. Pleasant air-conditioned shopping for mid-price to expensive branded goods and restaurants.

voyage.name: Soho and south of Hollywood Rd area
voyage.content: Has a trendy shopping area around Staunton and Lower Elgin St with lots of local designers.

voyage.name: The Lanes
voyage.content: Buy silks, fabrics, Chinese dresses, watches, leather bags and many other things here. Despite its prime location close to Central MTR, these narrow streets have a reputation among locals for quality goods at competitive prices.

voyage.name: Cat Street
voyage.content: Probably the best place to buy souvenirs, lots of Mao memorabilia, porcelain, Buddha statues and "antiques". Lok Ku Rd, walk down Hollywood Rd towards the west, when you see the Man Mo temple walk down the stairs on the right hand side.

voyage.name: Man Wa Lane
voyage.content: Also known a Chop Alley a multitude of little stalls offer everything from functional modern rubber stamps to hand carved traditional Chinese seals, you can pick out a stone seal and have it personalised with your name, your name in Chinese (many stores will have on display a list of popular transliterations of Western names into Chinese characters) your initials, or even your own design. The seal will be ready to co

voyage.name: Dumpling House
voyage.content: Great Beijing-style dumplings, avoid going there during lunch hour, because it is packed.

voyage.name: Good Luck Thai
voyage.content: Seating is both indoors and outdoors, very popular on weekends, nice atmosphere.

voyage.name: Law Fu Kee
voyage.content: Popular little restaurant serving congee and noodles.

voyage.name: Wai Kee Congee Shop
voyage.content: A good place to sample some traditional Hong Kong style food.

voyage.name: XTC Gelato
voyage.content: A popular place to get your fix of ice cream or frozen yoghurt.

voyage.name: Zhong Guo Song
voyage.address: Wo On Lane, Lan Kwai Fong
voyage.content: Good Chinese food, without MSG and less oil.

voyage.name: L16 Cafe and Bar
voyage.address: Hong Kong Park, 19 Cotton Tree Drive
voyage.content: Serves Thai and Italian food, but come for the location - not the food. A rare place to drink and eat outside away from the noise of Central.

voyage.name: Maxim's Palace
voyage.content: One of Hong Kong's most popular dim sum spots, featuring harbour views if you're lucky enough to score a window table. The atmosphere and food are very much in the classical dim sum tradition, a large, noisy hall with waitresses pushing around carts laden with goodies; try the siu mai (燒賣), har gao (蝦餃) and mango pudding. Dim sum served 11AM-3PM daily, expect to queue on Sundays (when the restaurant opens at 9AM). Tr

voyage.name: Pizza Express
voyage.content: Has a nice view overlooking the Mid-Levels Escalator.

voyage.name: Yung Kee Restaurant
voyage.content: This is a popular place for Cantonese-style roast goose and century eggs. Come early and make reservations as they have been known to run out of geese!

voyage.name: Baci
voyage.content: Pizza.

voyage.name: Beirut
voyage.content: Lebanese cuisine is top of the sheet. Lamb or chicken kebab and sisha. Nice decor but the food is a far cry from the real deal (particularly in taste).

voyage.name: Tokyo Joe
voyage.content: Japanese food.

voyage.name: Fung Shing Restaurant
voyage.content: Very local eatery known for its dim sum, which is cheap and good at $10 and up per serving. Open daily from 7:30AM for the dim sum breakfast crowd, but no English menu.

voyage.name: Al Dente
voyage.address: 16 Staunton St, Soho (中環蘇豪士丹頓街16號地下)
voyage.content: Italian cuisine. Serving large, medium quality dishes not too different from what you would find in an Italian bistro. Their pastas and meat dishes are better than their pizzas. Often full.

voyage.name: Ayuthaiya
voyage.address: 35 Hollywood Rd, Soho (中環荷李活道35號)
voyage.content: Thai cuisine. Serving quite authentic food in a stylish, dark environment.

voyage.name: Brunch Club
voyage.content: Neighbourhood-style Western coffee shop (pre-Starbucks style) specialising in brunch and breakfast, although dinner is also served. Customers are provided with a wide range of newspapers and magazines in English and Chinese. Clientele is mainly expatriate.

voyage.name: Double Happiness Cafe
voyage.content: Shanghai cuisine. Nice and simple little restaurant serving authentic Shanghainese dishes. Prices reflects that this is in the centre of Soho and comparable food can be found much cheaper elsewhere.

voyage.name: Jashan
voyage.content: Indian cuisine. Serves great curries and perfect naan. The lunch buffet is good value.

voyage.name: Oola
voyage.address: G/F, Centre Stage, Bridges St, Soho
voyage.content: Away from the crowds in Soho, but worth the extra walk. International menu in a comfortable environment. Serves as both a place to eat or drink. Drinks are expensive.

voyage.name: La Pampa
voyage.content: Argentinian.

voyage.name: The Peak Lookout
voyage.content: Serving a range of international cuisine such as naan bread, Hainan chicken, and steaks in a 19th-century heritage building. Also has a pleasant garden patio.

voyage.name: Percy Bakery
voyage.address: Shop b, g/f, 68 Catchick St, Kennedy Town
voyage.content: A high quality bakery. Take away and delivery service only.

voyage.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo Bombana
voyage.content: Only Italian restaurant outside Italy to be awarded three Michelin stars.

voyage.name: Bistro Bouchon
voyage.content: French bistro focusing on steaks.

voyage.name: Chez Patrick
voyage.content: An excellent, Parisian-style French restaurant. The proprietor, Patrick, has a delightful obsession with foie gras which extends to creative dishes such as foie gras ice cream served as a first course.

voyage.name: Chilli Fagara
voyage.content: Sichuan cuisine. Great spicy dishes including the favourites you will find in Sichuan Province. This restaurant's ambitions appear to go further than just making the food as the mainland original implying that some might be disappointed. Somewhat overpriced but still good.

voyage.name: Luk Yu Tea House
voyage.content: Famous for the excellent tea and traditional dim sum. It is a popular meeting place for businessmen. They provide an English menu on request.

voyage.name: Yung Kee Restaurant
voyage.content: Established in 1942, this restaurant has enjoyed unparalleled success and was once named in the "Top Fifteen Restaurants in the World" by Fortune Magazine. Previously a humble BBQ house serving its renowned roast goose, it has evolved into a world-famous Cantonese restaurant. Dim sum is also served at lunch-time. Be prepared for a noisy environment at peak times, this type of restaurant is not for those seeking a qui

voyage.name: HAHAClub
voyage.content: For cheaper booze, you can try here.

voyage.name: Works
voyage.content: A good place for tourists to start on the gay bar-scene. Popular with expats and tourists alike, it is easily accessible in Central. Friday and Saturday are the most popular nights but do not expect many drinkers to arrive much before 11PM.

voyage.name: 65 Peel
voyage.content: A bar with a very Hong Kong aesthetic serving cocktails and a range of locally brewed beer.

voyage.name: de België
voyage.content: A bar specialising in Belgian beers.

voyage.name: Craft Brew & Co
voyage.content: A corner bar with a selection of craft beer on tap.

voyage.name: The Globe
voyage.content: Excellent beer pub, also has good menu aimed at western taste buds. It is also one of the few places that has Typhoon T8 on tap, a locally produced cask ale.

voyage.name: Staunton's Wine Bar & Cafe
voyage.content: A western-style restaurant with a bar on the ground floor and table service upstairs.

voyage.name: Propaganda
voyage.content: Famous gay club. Tends to get going after Works has faded.

voyage.name: Bishop Lei International House
voyage.content: Operated by the Catholic Diocese.

voyage.name: Cosco Hotel
voyage.address: Yick Fung Garden, 20-21, Praya Rd, Kennedy Town

voyage.name: Jockey Club Mt. Davis Youth Hostel
voyage.address: Top of Mt Davis Path, Mt Davis, Kennedy Town
voyage.content: Great hostel almost at the top of Mt Davis, with good views over the city and plenty of fresh air, well away from the city bustle. Self-catering kitchen, with limited supplies sold in the hostel. Friendly staff.

voyage.name: Lan Kwai Fong Hotel @ Kau U Fong
voyage.content: A boutique hotel uniquely designed with a distinctive touch of oriental style. Each room's furniture, fabrics and artifacts are meticulously chosen displaying striking individuality. Awarded as "Asia's Leading Boutique Hotel" by World Travel Awards 2009.

voyage.name: Ovolo Hotel – 286 Queens Road Central
voyage.content: Boutique hotel that opened in 2012. 60 Rooms. Queen or twin mattresses, AppleTV, loot bag, rainfall shower, electric curtains, free minibar, free breakfast, free Wi-Fi, happy hour.

voyage.name: Hotel Jen
voyage.alt: 香港仁民饭店, formerly Traders Hotel
voyage.price: Listed rates from $1,243, discounted from $600, breakfast $152 (included for more expensive rooms)
voyage.content: Rooms with free internet and views of Victoria Harbour and nearby mountains. Business centre, fitness and outdoor swimming pool available. Chinese and Western restaurants as well as bar.

voyage.name: Mingle Place On The Wing
voyage.content: Full sized suite provides separate living/work and bedroom areas.

voyage.name: Ramada Hong Kong
voyage.price: Generally from $900, can be discounted to $600
voyage.address: 308 Des Voeux Rd West, Sai Ying Pun

voyage.name: ibis Hong Kong Central & Sheung Wan
voyage.address: 28 Des Voeux Road West, Sheung Wan
voyage.content: Hotel begins at 5th floor. Harbour view rooms available, good views of Kowloon. Breakfast buffet available. Midway between Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun MTR stations. Kennedy tram is also available. Macau Ferry Pier is a short walk away.

voyage.name: Conrad Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the conveniently located Pacific Place complex. 513 rooms, swimming pool, and health club. Amongst the five restaurants is Nicholini's.

voyage.name: Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.content: One of the most prestigious in Hong Kong, opened in 2005, 399 rooms, wall-to-wall windows with view of Victoria Harbour or Victoria Peak, two outdoor infinity pools, a spa, and a fitness centre. The only hotel in the world with two 3-star Michelin restaurants.

voyage.name: Island Shangri-La
voyage.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the conveniently located Pacific Place complex. The hotel comprises 531 rooms and 34 suites decorated with Asian-accented European furnishings. Facilities include a health club and swimming pool.

voyage.name: JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.content: One of three elegantly appointed 5-star hotels at the Pacific Place complex. Features 577 rooms, a swimming pool, 24-hour fitness centre, and six restaurants.

voyage.name: Landmark Mandarin Oriental
voyage.content: Boutique hotel, opened in 2005, 113 rooms, Oriental Spa.

voyage.name: Mandarin Oriental
voyage.content: The chain's original and prestigious flagship. 502 rooms, spa, indoor swimming pool, and fitness centre. Michelin 3-star chef Pierre Gagnaire has lent his name and inspiration to, Pierre, the hotel's French restaurant.

voyage.name: The Mercer
voyage.content: Opened in 2011, 55-room boutique hotel, outdoor swimming pool, 24-hour fitness centre with complementary minibar, coffee and tea.

voyage.name: Ovolo Hotel - 2 Arbuthnot road
voyage.content: Design boutique hotel with Apple TV, free 1Gbps Wi-Fi, free breakfast at cafe, full wash and dry services, free mini bar, free local calls, 24-hour gym and flexible checkout. Smoke free. Free access to 9000 citywide hotspots

voyage.name: Central Plaza
voyage.content: Can be seen from most of Wan Chai. Central Plaza was the tallest building in Asia from 1992 to 1996, and the tallest in Hong Kong until 2003. It is possible to tell the time by the changing lights on the top of this building. During business hours, you can take the lift from the ground floor to the sky lobby on the 46th floor to get a spectacular free view of the harbour and the island. Another option for a free is v

voyage.name: Noon Day Gun
voyage.content: The historic gun is fired every day at noon and once a year at midnight on New Year's Eve. To access the Noon Day Gun, enter the underground tunnel between the World Trade Centre and the Excelsior Hotel and follow the signs. Finding this tunnel is difficult and you might need to ask staff for directions. The tradition of firing a gun into Victoria Harbour everyday at noon dates back to the 1860s. It is believed that

voyage.name: Golden Bauhinia Square
voyage.content: The site of the ceremony in 1997 in which the United Kingdom returned Hong Kong to China. A flag raising ceremony is held here ever morning at 8AM, when the Hong Kong Police will perform foot drills and raise both the Chinese national flag and the Hong Kong flag to the accompaniment of the Chinese national anthem. Visit at night time for a stunning view of the neon-lit skylines of Kowloon and Hong Kong.

voyage.name: The Old Wan Chai Post Office
voyage.content: Now an Environmental Resource Centre, this building was used for over 70 years as a post office. This attractive building is the only declared monument in Wan Chai.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Central Library
voyage.content: Opened in 2001, Hong Kong's main public library looks over the playgrounds of Victoria Park. It is an impressive 12-storey structure that holds a vast collection of Chinese and English resources. Visitors will find exhibitions, wifi access, newspapers and magazines. There is a souvenir shop and a branch of Delifrance where you can relax.

voyage.name: Ammar Mosque and Osman Ramju Sadick Islamic Centre
voyage.address: No. 40, Oi Kwan Road, Wan Chai
voyage.content: The third mosque built in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Chai Wan Mosque
voyage.address: Cape Collison Road, Tai Tam Gap, Chai Wan
voyage.content: The fifth mosque built in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Fireboat Alexander Grantham Exhibition Gallery
voyage.content: Exhibits firefighting stuff.

voyage.name: The Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre
voyage.content: One of Hong Kong's most outstanding buildings. If you are refused admittance, you can take a walk along the promenade at the front of the building to find the place where the British returned Hong Kong to mainland China. Paved in concrete, the modest plaza where the Handover took place in 1997 is home to two monuments; one takes the form of a giant golden bauhinia and the other looks like a chimney stack. The bauhini

voyage.name: Hong Kong Film Archive
voyage.address: 50 Lei King Road, Sai Wan Ho

voyage.name: Law Uk Folk Museum
voyage.content: 18th-century Hakka village house.

voyage.name: The Museum of Coastal Defence
voyage.address: 175 Tung Hei Road, Shau Kei Wan
voyage.content: Despite its dry title, this museum is worth a visit if you enjoy military history.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Police Museum
voyage.content: There are five galleries: Orientation describing the history of the force, Triad Societies and Narcotics describing the history of Triad Societies and narcotic problems, Police Then & Now describing the transformation of Hong Kong Police Force over the years, Current Exhibition exhibiting changing themes, and Heroin Factory exhibiting a heroin production site.

voyage.name: Victoria Park
voyage.content: Take some time to walk through it or to watch people play football on three fields. There is also a jogging track through the park. Victoria Park can also be reached by MTR Exit B at Tin Hau station. During the summer months you can use the public open-air pool in Victoria Park. The pool costs $19 for adults ($9 kids) and payment can be made by coins or Octopus card.

voyage.name: Quarry Bay Park
voyage.content: A good place to walk that provides an alternative view of the eastern end of the harbour, instead of the familiar one of the west. It also serves as a connection between SOHO east (a reasonably attractive restaurant and pub area) and Cityplaza shopping centre.

voyage.name: Southorn Playground
voyage.alt: 修頓遊樂場, 修頓球場
voyage.content: Amidst the skyscrapers of Wan Chai, Southorn Playground offers a scarce area of public outdoor space for football, basketball and has seating for those who just want to relax and watch.

voyage.name: Gloucester Road
voyage.content: Pronounced in the British way as Gloss-ter Road, this street is famous for car showrooms where the rich will spend and the rest will take photographs of themselves in front of their dream car.

voyage.name: Horse racing
voyage.content: Horse racing has been taking place at Happy Valley racetrack since 1846. Happy Valley is particularly impressive during the evening meets with the surrounding skyscrapers lit up. Unless you know the right sort of people your best chance of getting into the races is by the public entrance. Entrance will cost you just a few dollars and you will have the advantage of being at ground level next to the race track. Alcohol

voyage.name: Hong Kong Racing Museum
voyage.address: 2/F, Happy Valley Stand, Happy Valley Racecourse, Wong Nai Chung Rd, Happy Valley
voyage.content: Artificats and some of the largest exhibits in the world next to the track of the Happy Valley Racecourse.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts
voyage.address: The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts 1 Gloucester Road Wanchai
voyage.content: A venue for dance, music and drama.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Cricket Club
voyage.content: Private club but one restaurant is open to the public. If you're a cricket player, you can apply to join as a sports member.

voyage.name: Sogo
voyage.content: A Japanese department store. As well as the standard fare of international label goods (clothes, electronics, home furnishings, etc), there is an excellent supermarket in the basement, which sells a variety of Asian foods.

voyage.name: Times Square
voyage.content: A shopping centre in Causeway Bay with an excellent concentration of mid-price range shops and restaurants. CitySuper in the basement is one of Hong Kong's upmarket supermarkets, with a food court serving a variety of reasonably priced meals.

voyage.name: Hysan Place
voyage.content: High-end shopping mall with a food court on upper floor.

voyage.name: Cityplaza
voyage.address: 18 Taikoo Shing Road, Sai Wan Ho
voyage.content: A large shopping centre, with an ice-skating rink.

voyage.name: Chinese Goods Centre Ltd
voyage.content: Forget the westernised shopping malls and head for this Chinese-style department store in North Point. Here you will find almost anything you might expect in a large department store except prices are extremely competitive. If you are looking to buy gifts with an oriental flavour this is worth a try.

voyage.name: Chun Yeung Street
voyage.content: A local market near the North Point Tram terminus. You can find traditional Chinese food, especially Hokkien style food there. There is a variety of household items, clothes and fresh food there. It is a bazaar typical of many on Hong Kong Island.

voyage.name: G.O.D
voyage.address: Sharp Street, East Entrance, Causeway Bay
voyage.content: G.O.D. is a play on the Cantonese slang for "to live better". Here you will find a range of designer gifts and household items.

voyage.name: Fashion Walk
voyage.content: An indoor street with shops and a range of western and Asian restaurants.

voyage.name: RC Outfitters
voyage.address: 2/F, Kin Tak Fung Commercial Bldg, 467-473 Hennessy Road, Causeway Bay
voyage.content: A good range of hiking and camping accessories, plus outdoor clothing at reasonable prices.

voyage.name: Wan Chai Computer Centre
voyage.content: Although not the largest computer centre in Hong Kong, this one is above Wan Chai station with two floors of small shops selling computers, laptops, tablet, accessories, headphones, games, etc. It is also the easiest to get to on Hong Kong island. Some shops open from 10:30, although generally speaking it isn't worth to visit before midday.

voyage.name: Chiu Yuen
voyage.content: Small and usually packed eatery serving up a wide range of simple fare, but the crowd-pullers are the beef brisket noodles (a scarcely believable $13) and the homemade giant fishball soup ($16). Other branches are in Aberdeen and Causeway Bay.

voyage.name: Tsui Wah Restaurant
voyage.content: Clean and multilingual, this is a moderately priced cha chaan teng where even a non-Chinese speaker can easily explore. Aside from the typical cha chaan teng foods such as French toast, curry, baked rice, fried noodles, and Hong Kong style milk-tea, also try their famous fishball noodle in soup. Expect to share a table at peak hours.

voyage.name: Cafe Kenon
voyage.address: Shop 208, 2/F Tai Yau Plaza, 181 Johnston Rd, Wanchai
voyage.content: Where affordable Italian food meets Chinese expectations.

voyage.name: Tai Hing Roast Restaurant
voyage.address: G/F, Shop J, Po Ming Bldg, 49-57 Lee Garden Rd, Causeway Bay.
voyage.content: A Cantonese BBQ eatery. Roast pork, roast piglet, BBQ pork, roast goose, soy sauce chicken are all hanging in the front display window, available to eat in or take out.

voyage.name: Loving Hut
voyage.address: Shops B&C, G/F, The Hennessy, 256 Hennessy Rd
voyage.content: Serving vegetarian and vegan fast food at affordable prices.

voyage.name: New Bangkok Restaurant
voyage.content: Friendly staff serving excellent Thai food.

voyage.name: Hokkaido Dairy Farm
voyage.address: Shop A-B, G/F, 211 Johnston Road, Wan Chai
voyage.content: Ham, eggs, toast and Japanese milk. Very good for a light breakfast or lunch.

voyage.name: 3.6.9. Restaurant Shanghai
voyage.content: Great old style dive usually packed with locals especially at lunch. Shanghai style Chinese food, excellent and inexpensive Xaio Long Bao. About as authentic as you'll find in this part of the island.

voyage.name: Baby Blue Cafe and Bar
voyage.address: 3/F, Chuang's Enterprises Building, 382 Lockhart Road, Causeway Bay
voyage.content: Western food served to meet Hong Kong taste buds.

voyage.name: The Quarterdeck Club
voyage.content: Fenwick Pier, Wanchai. This is one of the few harbourside restaurants. Slightly spoiled by the land reclamation nearby

voyage.name: The Flying Pan
voyage.content: On the corner of Lockhart Road and Luard Road. Look above Mes Amis and you will find the best place for breakfast and it's open all-day, everyday. This is the place where you can have a full-English washed down with a glass of lager at any time you prefer. It has an extensive menu catering for all preferences and a "frequent fryer" club if you want to keep going back. Staff are friendly and speak good English.

voyage.name: Kung Tak Lam
voyage.content: A delightful vegetarian restaurant serving Shanghainese cuisine. Hotpot, dim sum and noodles dishes are made with MSG free ingredients.

voyage.name: Chun Kee Restaurant
voyage.address: 117-119 Shau Kei Wan Road, Sai Wan Ho
voyage.content: Serves typical Chinese food from dumplings to Peking Duck.

voyage.name: Red Pepper Restaurant
voyage.content: Causeway Bay (MTR: Causeway Bay). Sichuan cuisine; spicy dishes.

voyage.name: Pho Saigon
voyage.content: Extremely good Vietnamese restaurant serving traditional dishes including Pho and Vietnamese coffee. Expect to pay around $120.

voyage.name: Tai Ping Koon Restaurant
voyage.content: (太平館餐廳), 6 Pak Sha Road, Causeway Bay. Founded in Guangzhou in 1860, the three locations (two in Kowloon) have now become institutions of Canto-Western cuisine. Don't be put off by the touristy menu available in three languages, as the restaurant is very popular with locals. Some specialties are the Swiss sauce chicken wings, roasted young pigeon, smoked promfret, dried fried rice noodles with beef, and baked souffle

voyage.name: Café One
voyage.content: Causeway Bay, Open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Fun & friendly informal dining from an open kitchen and an exciting buffet featuring a wide selection of Asian and Western cuisines.

voyage.name: Tony Roma's
voyage.content: International food. This branch has the advantage of an outdoor terrace that enables you to eat and drink above the noise of the streets below.

voyage.name: Under the Bridge Spicy Crab
voyage.address: Shop 1-2, G/F, 414 - 424 Jaffe Road, Causeway Bay
voyage.content: This has become a Hong Kong institution that is famous for its Typhoon Shelter style crab. People come for the food not the interior which is basic.

voyage.name: West Villa Restaurant
voyage.alt: 5 minutes walk from exit D2 of Taikoo Shing MTR
voyage.content: Its signature dim sum is the cha xiu bao (叉燒包) or roast pork buns that is served steamed, fried or as rolls. One of the items is named "Big Brother Chaxiu" after Hong Kong's film star Jacky Chan (Big Brother) who is fond of its cha xiu buns.

voyage.name: Cosmo Hotel Wan Chai
voyage.content: This hotel is spanned across 23 floors and consists of 142 rooms and suites. Free shuttle bus services are provided for 15 locations. They also offer free use of smart phone, 4G internet, Wi-Fi, local and IDD calls to 9 countries.

voyage.name: Fook Lam Moon
voyage.content: The main branch of an old school Cantonese restaurant group with locations in Kowloon, Shanghai and Japan. Famous for luxurious delicacies such as abalone, and swallow's nest. More affordable specialties include roast suckling pig, crispy chicken, and steamed lotus leaf rice.

voyage.name: The Coffee Academics
voyage.address: G/F, Bigfoot Centre, 38 Yiu Wa St
voyage.content: Great coffee a short walk from Times Square in Causeway bay. Coffee is roasted on premise and they have an outside sitting area.

voyage.name: The Cafe Corridor
voyage.content: Small coffee shop directly opposite Time Square. Entrance is really small so look carefully. Good coffee for $26.

voyage.name: Café "1974"
voyage.address: G/F, ICAC Building, 303 Java Road, North Point
voyage.content: A coffee shop operated by Po Leung Kuk that also functions as the ICAC's museum. The shop was named after the year of establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, and coffee is known to be one of the drinks available to detainees during interrogation. Good coffee at around $22.

voyage.name: The Pawn
voyage.content: Wan Chai. A Western-style bar and cafe in an attractive building that was once a pawn shop. It is away from the naughty parts of Wan Chai in one of the few historic buildings remaining in Hong Kong. It will appeal to visitors seeking a good range of imported beers and wines.

voyage.name: Joe Bananas
voyage.content: This is one Hong Kong's most famous and popular bars, and can be highly recommended to younger travellers. Drinks are competitively priced, and staff are helpful and friendly.

voyage.name: Devils Advocate
voyage.content: Popular with the rugby crowd with English pub food.

voyage.name: Kangaroo Pub
voyage.content: Australian sports bar. Has a book exchange.

voyage.name: Carnegie's
voyage.content: Rock music themed bar. Live bands playing occasionally, sports on multiple screens and a big screen, dancing the night away on the bar top.

voyage.name: The Canny Man
voyage.content: Scottish style Whiskey Bar with a free pool table.

voyage.name: Skitz Sports Bar
voyage.content: 5/F. Sports bar with pool tables, darts and big screens.

voyage.name: The Wanch
voyage.content: A good bar for music lovers with live music playing every night. There is also a showcase of local bands held over several days around the 1st of July every year.

voyage.name: The Chapel
voyage.content: Serves curry.

voyage.name: The Jockey
voyage.content: A relaxed British style pub that serves food. When the weather suits this is a great place to sit outside and watch the world pass by.

voyage.name: Inn Side Out
voyage.content: Also 'East End Brewing Company'.

voyage.name: Moon Garden Tea House
voyage.content: A calming location in a busy part of town where you can choose from over 70 types of tea and, for a price, enjoy the Chinese ritual of tea served in tiny cups. Food is also served.

voyage.name: Dickens Bar
voyage.content: Popular British-style sports bar in the basement of the Excelsior hotel. A good range of drinks and serves very good English food, including a notable curry lunch buffet.

voyage.name: Wang Fat Hostel
voyage.address: 3rd floor, block A, 47 Paterson St., Causeway Bay
voyage.content: This hostel would go out of business competing against any hostel in any European city, but compared to the prisons of Chunking and Mirador Mansions, it's halfway decent. Single rooms go for $250-300 and dorms run about $170. There is one dingy kitchen and a few refrigerators. The staff are brusque but helpful and honest, and there is free wireless and a single molasses-slow computer with free internet for hostel gue

voyage.name: Yesinn Hostel
voyage.address: Flat B, 5th floor, Front Block, 294 King's Rd., Causeway Bay, Hong
voyage.content: The youth & budget hostel in Hong Kong Island. Provide Mix/Female Dorms and private rooms for backpackers, young people, internship and budget business travellers who are looking for a warm, local, homely atmosphere and an affordable quality hostel.Private rooms go from HK$260 and dorms run from HK$99.

voyage.name: Sun Kong Hostel
voyage.content: Block C, sixth floor. A few minutes walk from Causeway Bay MTR Station (exit E). Rooms are small but clean with daily maid service. There is a communal refrigerator for roughly ever eight rooms. Toilets tend to block rather easy though. Double rooms run at about $300 with singles being anything from $130 with a shared toilet to between $200 and $400 with a private one.

voyage.name: Ibis North Point
voyage.content: This inexpensive Ibis offers really tiny rooms in a 31-floor high building. The view towards the harbour is rather nice.

voyage.name: Walden Hotel
voyage.content: Walden Hotel is a 3-star business and leisure hotel which offers 54 guest rooms. Well equipped bedrooms include a desk area, tea and coffee making facilities, LCD television with satellite TV channels, full amenities, mini bar and free In-room Internet service.

voyage.name: Lanson Place Hotel
voyage.content: Lanson Place Hotel is five to 10 minutes walk from the MTR system. It's 20 minutes away from Central by taxi, and 20 minutes from Kowloon by MTR. If you want to take a breather, Vistoria Park is five minutes walk. Some of their in-room amenities include an LCD flat screen TV, wireless broadband Internet connection, and a personal safe. As for guest service, they provide 24-hour reception, concierge service, business

voyage.name: Cosmo Hotel
voyage.content: This hotel spans across 23 floors and consists of 142 colour-coded rooms and suites and offers green amenities, free Wi-Fi up to 200 mbps, provides a smart phone with 4G Internet access and free shuttle services for 15 destinations.

voyage.name: Mingle Place By The Park
voyage.content: In the heart of Wanchai next to parks, public facilities, shopping centres, historical sites and close to the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. The hotel has a business centre.

voyage.name: Novotel Hong Kong Century
voyage.content: A fairly reasonable 4-star hotel in the heart of Wanchai.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Express
voyage.content: Comfortable, clean and next to the shopping action in Times Square. Breakfast has Western and Chinese options, with the Western options decidedly underwhelming. Internet is fast.

voyage.name: Dorsett Wanchai Hotel
voyage.content: An environmentally friendly “green” hotel having 454 superior rooms, premier rooms, grand deluxe course view rooms and suites. The hotel offers free Wi-Fi up to 200 Mbps, walk-in massage shower with rain shower head and coffee and tea-making facilities.

voyage.name: Somerset Victoria Park Hong Kong
voyage.content: This property offers studio and one-bedroom apartments, equipped with complimentary Wi-Fi and a smartphone with 3G data.

voyage.name: Metropark Hotel Wanchai, Hong Kong
voyage.content: The 4-star hotel underwent a multi-billion major renovation, representing a new and refreshing image. In heart of the city, equipped with LCD TV and broadband service.

voyage.name: Grand Hyatt Hong Kong
voyage.content: Overlooks Victoria Harbour. Has a direct connection to the Hong Kong Conventions and Exhibition Centre. Host to the renowned Plateau Spa.

voyage.name: Lanson Place Hotel
voyage.content: Causeway Bay. A small boutique hotel in a modern building with an old world European facade. Situated in a "less-busy" corner of Causeway Bay.

voyage.name: Jia Boutique Hotel
voyage.content: Causeway Bay. A 54-room boutique hotel designed by Philippe Starck. Complimentary in-room broadband internet access, breakfast, wine during cocktail hour, afternoon cakes, and California Fitness gym access. Some rooms with cooking equipment.

voyage.name: The Park Lane Hong Kong
voyage.content: Causeway Bay. This 810-room 4-star hotel may not be brand new, but it is in the heart of Hong Kong's shopping and entertainment district. Great views of either Victoria Harbour or Victoria Park. From $1380.

voyage.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Clock Tower
voyage.alt: 尖沙咀鐘樓, Former Kowloon-Canton Railway Clock Tower
voyage.content: Built out of red bricks and granite, the Clock Tower peaks at 44 metres, and is topped by a 7-metre lightning rod. The top of the tower can be reached by a wooden staircase located within.

voyage.name: Avenue of Stars
voyage.content: A promenade to honour celebrities of the Hong Kong film industry, modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

voyage.name: A Symphony of Lights
voyage.content: The narration is in English M-W-F, Mandarin Tu-Th-Sa and Cantonese Su. You can also download the app for your preferred narration.

voyage.name: Dialogue in the Dark
voyage.price: Weekdays $160, $90 for students and seniors; weekends $180, $100 for students and seniors
voyage.address: Shop 215, 2/F, The Household Centre, Nob Hill, 8 King Lai Path, Mei Foo
voyage.content: An exhibition in complete darkness. Experience five different Hong Kong themed environments using your non-visual senses on a 75-minute tour with the help of a visually impaired guide. Reservations are recommended, especially for a tour in English or Mandarin instead of Cantonese.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Cultural Centre
voyage.content: Opened in 1989 and in a prominent position on the waterfront, it is a contender for being the most famous ugly building in Hong Kong. However, if you are a lover of the arts, don't judge this building by its bland exterior; inside the architects have created a superb space that really does justice to the sights and sounds of each performance.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Heritage Discovery Centre
voyage.address: Kowloon Park, Haiphong Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: Housed in former British colonial barracks, which are architecturally interesting in their own right. The centre houses one permanent (Explore our Heritage) and a couple of temporary exhibitions about Hong Kong's and China's history. There are also lectures, workshops and similar events.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
voyage.content: A fascinating, strange and elusive place. The entrance lies up one floor, mimicking the “temple” approach to the high altar of culture and art. Once you arrive on the first floor, you are bathed in light from the wall of glass that gives you a panoramic view of Hong Kong Island. The objects on show are Chinese ceramics, terracotta, rhinoceros horn and Chinese paintings. There is also a temporary exhibition space devo

voyage.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
voyage.address: 100 Chatham Rd South, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: The permanent exhibition, the Hong Kong Story, covers the history of Hong Kong from millions of years ago until the reunification with China in 1997. Exhibits are about the nature, culture and history of Hong Kong. Also special exhibitions changing every few months. Forget the idea that all of Hong Kong museums are frumpy and boring. The Hong Kong Story is a real must go and do, ideal for those who want to make sense

voyage.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
voyage.price: Adults $50, concessions $25, entry is free on Wednesdays provided you book online
voyage.hours: Mon Wed Thu 10AM-6PM, Fri Sat Sun 10AM-8PM
voyage.address: 8 Museum Drive, West Kowloon Cultural District (西九文化區博物館道8號)
voyage.content: A museum displaying artefacts from the Forbidden City in Beijing.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Science Museum
voyage.address: 2 Science Museum Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui East
voyage.content: Large museum with many interactive exhibits including an energy machine and an airplane. A museum which decided to make an architectural statement about its purpose, yet somehow got it horribly wrong. This museum is primarily aimed at children. The maths puzzles and optical illusions on the top floor are challenging. There is a giant Rube Goldberg machine spanning the entire museum that is run for a few minutes every

voyage.name: Hong Kong Space Museum
voyage.price: $10 on most days. Free on Wednesdays
voyage.hours: Mon Wed-Sat noon-8:45PM, Sun 10AM-8:45PM, Tue closed
voyage.content: Small museum, with a basic history of space flight in static exhibits, including a single exhibit on Chinese space flight. It also has interactive exhibits, allowing you to fly a hang glider, work a space motion system, and simulate walking on the moon. It has a planetarium attached that shows movies projected onto the roof. Plan ahead if you want to see an English session, as most are Cantonese. It is fun for kids a

voyage.name: Lei Cheng Uk Han Tomb Museum
voyage.content: Tomb from the Eastern Han dynasty (AD 25 - 220) discovered in 1955. Exhibition hall displaying pottery and artifacts from the excavation of the tomb.

voyage.name: M+
voyage.content: Museum of contemporary visual culture (architecture, design, animation, and visual art) with a local and global focus.

voyage.name: Kowloon Park
voyage.content: the location of a former British barrack. There, you will find not only pleasant gardens, but aviaries, museums, and sporting facilities, including Hong Kong's best swimming pool complex, which offers both indoor and outdoor pools. A wide range of swimming, diving and children's play-pools will appeal to kids of all ages, and their frazzled parents who are seeking a safe place for youngsters to play away from the tra

voyage.name: Kowloon Walled City Park
voyage.address: Tung Tau Tsuen Road, Kowloon City
voyage.content: The Kowloon Walled City began as an enclave that remained under Chinese sovereignty when the New Territories and the rest of Kowloon were ceded to the British. After the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912, its legal status became disputed, and there was no effective government within the walled city as a result. The massive influx of mainland Chinese refugees after the communist takeover led to haphazard construction o

voyage.name: Nan Lian Garden
voyage.content: A Tang-dynasty-style garden, part of the Chi Lin Nunnery complex.

voyage.name: Shek Kip Mei Estate
voyage.content: Built in the 1950s, this is one of the few remaining places where you can grasp the living conditions of Hong Kong during the 50s and 60s. Despite the march of progress promulgated by the Urban Renewal Authority, there are still a few blocks of flats remaining from the 1950s, which are still occupied. Walk from Shek Kip Mei MTR Station.

voyage.name: Shanghai Street
voyage.content: runs north-south parallel to Nathan Road and offers an easy to navigate urban transect. Start at the north-side of Kowloon Park and wander up to Langham Place, a modern shopping and hotel complex which is next to Mong Kok MTR station. Along the way you will experience Kowloon in its raw authenticity. This is not your regular tourist trail, but crumbling tenements and small-scale industrial and commercial outfits blur

voyage.name: Marine Police Headquarters
voyage.content: Dating back to 1884, it is an attractive colonial building that has been renovated to become a major tourism attraction with shops and restaurants.

voyage.name: Sik Sik Yuen Wong Tai Sin Temple
voyage.content: Next to Wong Tai Sin MTR Station, this is the most popular Taoist temple in Hong Kong. This is where many people ask for divine guidance by a practice known as kau cim (求籤), a practice that has all but disappeared in mainland China. Entrance is free, though voluntary donations are welcome.

voyage.name: Kowloon Mosque and Islamic Centre
voyage.alt: 九龍清真寺暨伊斯蘭中心
voyage.address: No. 105, Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: The largest mosque in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Kowloon Park Swimming Pool Complex
voyage.content: Offers a wide range of services, including an indoors Olympic-sized pool, a slightly smaller training pool, a diving pool, and a leisure pool for younger swimmers. During the summer months, the indoor pools are air-conditioned, whilst in winter the water is heated. During the summer season, there are four outdoor leisure pools that are popular with teenagers, but all age-groups make good use of the pools. A limited n

voyage.name: Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground
voyage.alt: Mission Road Ground, 天光道遊樂場
voyage.address: Tin Kwong Rd, Ma Tau Wai
voyage.content: With a capacity of 3500, this is the home stadium of the Hong Kong national cricket team, who play separately from China.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Coliseum
voyage.content: Multi-purpose indoor arena with 12,500 seats. A famous landmark shaped almost like an upside down pyramid. Used for sport events, concerts and other things.

voyage.name: Elements
voyage.address: 1 Austin Road West, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: Opened in 2007, Elements is Hong Kong's latest mega-mall. Aimed at wealthy shoppers, it has five themed shopping zones: Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth. Owned by the MTR Corporation, the shops are located above Kowloon MTR station. Probably not worth going out of your way for, but it does have some of the most extravagant public toilets in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Festival Walk
voyage.content: Festival Walk is another excellent shopping mall in the suburb of Kowloon Tong. A very pleasant place to shop, similar to Pacific Place but catering more to locals.

voyage.name: Langham Place
voyage.content: Langham Place is an entertainment complex comprising of a 15-storey shopping mall, a 59-level Grade A office tower and the 5-star Langham Place Hotel. Over 300 shops where you will find everything from fashion labels to casual wear, from accessories to electronics. On special occasions, large crowds will gather under the 'Digital Sky' to celebrate festive events such as the New Year's Eve countdown. Throughout the ye

voyage.name: Lok Fu Centre
voyage.content: Located in a public housing estate, goods here are generally more affordable than in other places. There is also a large department store here.

voyage.name: Harbour City
voyage.content: The largest shopping mall in Hong Kong. It is next to the Star Ferry pier. There are shops of almost any description there. The goods are mostly mid price range to high price brand name goods. The views of the bay are especially good from here at night.

voyage.name: Nathan Road
voyage.content: Tsim Sha Tsui's main artery. Packed with stores, particularly cheap electronics shops. Be careful when shopping here; these slippery guys know every trick in the book and some stores are notorious for overcharging tourists. Locals seldom go to Tsim Sha Tsui for electronic products. It is more advisable to go to Mong Kok or Sham Shui Po instead.

voyage.name: Temple Street Night Market
voyage.content: Encompasses a block of streets in Kowloon barricaded at the end of each day with stalls selling almost anything until midnight. You can buy the usual touristy stuff, but there are also bargains like Chinese silk pajamas, toys, electronics and cheap leather goods. Arrive at Yau Ma Tei MTR Station Exit C, then walk up Man Ming Lane to Temple Street after nightfall. Be prepared to bargain vigorously as there are no fixe

voyage.name: Mong Kok
voyage.content: With a population density of 130,000/km2, Mong Kok is described as the busiest district in the world. It is characterised by a mixture of old and new multi-story buildings, with shops and restaurants at street level, and commercial or residential units above. (The shops on upper floors, which tourists may miss, often sell things cheaper.) Many of Mong Kok's streets have acquired nicknames reflecting the specialties o

voyage.name: Tung Choi Street
voyage.address: Tung Choi St, between Sai Yeung Choi St and Fa Yuen St
voyage.content: Hong Kong's biggest outdoor shopping experience. Prices here may not be the cheapest, as the area is popular with tourists, but the variety, chaos and sheer number of sellers is mind-boggling and well worth the visit. It is also opened during daytime, unlike the nearby Temple Street Night Market. As with other markets lacking fixed prices, those perceived as being tourists will be quoted a higher price—so bring your

voyage.name: Sai Yeung Choi Street South
voyage.content: A street full of shops selling consumer electronic products, cosmetics, and discount books.

voyage.name: Yuen Po Street Bird Garden
voyage.content: Hundreds of songbirds in exquisitely crafted cages can be seen at this market.

voyage.name: Fa Yuen Street
voyage.address: Fa Yuen St, between Boundary St and Dundas St
voyage.content: This street is famous for selling sport gear, with over fifty stores selling sport shoes.

voyage.name: Goldfish Street
voyage.content: Dozens of shops selling tropical freshwater and marine fish, aquariums and accessories.

voyage.name: Flower Market Road
voyage.content: The street and the nearby side streets are packed with florists and street vendors selling flowers and plants. Worth a visit even if shrubs aren't high on your shopping list.

voyage.name: Cheung Sha Wan Road
voyage.content: Famous for garments. There are many shops selling clothes along Cheung Sha Wan Road. It is within walking distance from Sham Shui Po MTR Station. A number of bus routes also pass along Cheung Sha Wan Road.

voyage.name: Sham Shui Po
voyage.content: Has the largest number of computer and electronics shops.

voyage.name: Golden Computer Centre
voyage.content: The largest computer mall in Hong Kong, with both hardware and software vendors competing extremely vigorously. This is a Mecca for the nerdy-trainspotter-types who salivate over the latest gadget.

voyage.name: Apliu Street
voyage.address: Apliu St, between Yen Chow St and Nam Cheong St
voyage.content: A collection of market stalls where you can find phones, small electronic devices and DIY tools. Even if you are not that interested in electronic bric-à-brac, the pedestrianised streets in the area have a buzz about them that make a visit interesting.

voyage.name: Sin Tat Shopping Centre
voyage.content: If you're after a new phone, this mall is home to many sellers with a wide selection, from iPhones to Japanese imports.

voyage.name: Temple Street
voyage.content: South of Mong Kok is a great place to eat Chinese street food. You have not been to Honkers unless you have eaten in this street. Temple Street, famously featured in Chinese cinema, is one of the few pedestrianised streets in Kowloon where you can sit, relax and watch the world pass by. Seafood is a popular choice, but most restaurants will provide you with an extensive English/Chinese menu that caters for most taste

voyage.name: Chungking Mansions
voyage.content: Houses many budget Indian, Nepali and African restaurants. Touts at the front entrance will lead you to the restaurants via the small rickety lifts. Be warned that the competition between the touts can become very open, sometimes aggressive, so you should be prepared to make your choice as quickly as possible to avoid being dragged away to a restaurant that you did not really plan on going to. Chungking Mansions is o

voyage.name: CitySuper
voyage.address: 3/F, Gateway Arcade, Harbour City, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: A local upscale supermarket chain with pan Asian, Western style food and has its own food court in Harbour City on Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui.

voyage.name: Choi Lung Restaurant
voyage.content: A typical local Chinese restaurant offering dim sum and a Cantonese style dinner. Dim Sum starts from $4.80. It is a nightclub after seven with contemporary music.

voyage.name: Dragon Centre Food Court
voyage.address: 8/F, Dragon Centre, 37K Yen Chow Street, Sham Shui Po
voyage.content: This food court provides a variety of Chinese, Southeast Asian and Western cuisines at attractive prices. Dishes range from $10 up.

voyage.name: Fa Yuen Street Complex
voyage.content: A complex consisting of a wet market, cooked food centre, sports centre and a public library. It is a place where you can find cheap and genuine Hong Kong style food in Kowloon. There was only one small food stall open on a Sunday afternoon. Maybe better during the week?

voyage.name: Mr. Wong's
voyage.content: This one is popular with exchange students in Hong Kong, offering all the food you can eat and all the beer you can drink.

voyage.name: Swagat
voyage.content: On the first floor of Chungking Mansions, this is arguably one of the best Indian restaurants in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Tim Ho Wan
voyage.content: It is said to be the cheapest Michelin starred restaurant in the world, serving a variety of dim sum dishes starting at $10. Be prepared to wait one, two or even three hours if you come on a busy day (you get a numbered menu/ticket and can come back later).

voyage.name: Jade Palace
voyage.address: 4/F, Star House, Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: A tasty and tourist-friendly dim sum spot. Order by selecting from a card (also in English), not from a cart. Try the shrimp and chive dumplings and the tripe in ginger soup. Dim sum served 11AM-3PM daily, dishes $16-40 each.

voyage.name: Red Ant
voyage.address: G/F, 27 Ashley Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: A modern bistro-like restaurant with a wide selection of light meals and snacks. No alcohol is served but there is a long list of fresh juices and teas.

voyage.name: Yat Tung Heen
voyage.address: Eaton Hotel, 380 Nathan Road, Kwun Chung
voyage.content: Cantonese dishes and dim sum, from traditional favourites to original creations.

voyage.name: Aberdeen Seafood Restaurant
voyage.price: Eat outside on the pavement and watch the world pass you buy in this busy street for pedestrians. Serves goose and other meat dishes in addition to seafood. A cheap place to drink beer

voyage.name: Green
voyage.content: Contemporary cafe and restaurant located within the modern Hotel Icon. Lunch offers set menus with lobster, pasta and more. Nice desserts and wine list. The interior is beautiful, with one of the world's largest indoor vertical gardens.

voyage.name: La Taverna Restaurant
voyage.content: Hong Kong's oldest Italian restaurant sits hidden in plain view at the end of busy Ashley Road. Stepping through the door is like stepping back in time to a Hong Kong of the past or at least an Italian version of it circa 1960s. Delicious pastas and meat dishes and risottos to die for. Well worth a visit as much as for a sense of Hong Kong history as the tasty Italian food. A true oasis of tranquility in bustling Kow

voyage.name: Oi Man Sang
voyage.address: Sham Shui Po Building, 1A-1C Shek Kip Mei St
voyage.content: This outdoor kitchen may be the last outdoor food stall still cooking over the extreme heat of kerosene, wok hei-style. Expect to stand in line for a bit.

voyage.name: Fook Lam Moon
voyage.content: The yum cha/dim sum is excellent. The service and decor is also impressive. Expect to pay around $55 per serve for the mid range dishes. The English menu is only a small subset of the Chinese menu so take along someone who can translate to increase your choice of dishes. Another

voyage.name: Gaddi's
voyage.address: Peninsula Hotel, Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: Arguably Hong Kong's leading restaurant that has delighted aficionados of French food and wine for over 80 years. This is the place where you can test your own command of the French language against French-speaking Chinese waiters. You will be disappointed if you are expecting great harbour views.

voyage.name: Morton's The Steakhouse
voyage.content: The Hong Kong location for this famous chain of American steakhouses, Morton's has one best in the city multiple times. With views overlooking the harbour, great service and classic cocktails - combined with thick steaks - makes Morton's a classy and classic experience.

voyage.name: Nobu
voyage.content: The HK location for this exclusive Japanese restaurant. Nobu has delicate bento box lunches and decadent dinners and desserts. Remarkable service and drinks, and a view overlooking the Harbour that is worth the price. Dress nice and make a reservation if going for dinner.

voyage.name: Aqua
voyage.content: Nearby at the top of the 1 Peking Road office building is an alternative and less touristy spot with equally impressive views. As well as a bar, they have a Japanese and Italian restaurant for those without a budget.

voyage.name: Biergarten
voyage.content: This friendly German bar is one of the few places in Kowloon where you can find a good range of quality beers. Excellent German food is served — not just sausages and sauerkraut. Use Exit N2 at East Tsim Sha Tsui MTR station.

voyage.name: Felix
voyage.content: Atop the Peninsula Hotel on Salisbury Rd, is known for its Philippe Starck interior and the views of the harbour skyline, whilst the men's bathroom has an impressive view up Nathan Road. According to legend, the world's first screwdriver was mixed up here, sampling this simple mix of orange juice and vodka will set you back around $100 a pop.

voyage.name: Hutong
voyage.content: Hutong is a great place to get a good view of Hong Kong from the top floor of a business building. It's a Michelin starred restaurant with amazing food — try the signature crispy lamb breast with garlic and ginger.

voyage.name: Knutsford Terrace
voyage.content: Near the Miramar hotel is perhaps best described as the 'Lang Kwai Fong' of Kowloon, and has a large number of bars and restaurants of variable quality that cater for mid-range budgets. A little smaller and less phrenetic than Lan Kwai Fong, but well worth the effort to poke your nose along this narrow street on a Saturday evening.

voyage.name: Ashley Road
voyage.content: Between Nathan Road and the Ocean Terminal shopping mall, features many Western restaurants and bars.

voyage.name: Mody Road/Centennial Garden
voyage.content: Close to many good hotels, this area of Tsim Sha Tsui offers a more relaxed environment for a drink. Here you will find bars and restaurants spilling out onto the pavement. Leave East Tsim Sha Tsui station at Exit P1, and head past the Kowloon Shangri-La hotel.

voyage.name: Tung Choi Street
voyage.content: Between Prince Edward Road and Boundary Street, is one of Kowloon's up-and-coming bar strips. Few tourists or expats venture here, but there are nearly two dozen bars. Some specialize in karaoke while others have open fronts and extensive drink menus. Prince Edward MTR, exit A.

voyage.name: Australian guesthouse
voyage.content: A clean guesthouse with TV, good Wi-Fi, fridge, hot water, air con and en suite bathroom. The rooms seem to be quite modern and updated although fairly small. Owner is a pretty nice and helpful guy. Room was cleaned and made up every day. Hot water is pretty strong and good! The beds in the twin rooms (sleeps 2) go for about $250.

voyage.name: Canadian Hostel
voyage.address: 7th floor Chungking Mansions, Block E, Flat E6
voyage.content: Clean guesthouse with TV, fast Wi-Fi, 24 hours cold and hot water. All the rooms are air conditioned and have en suite bathrooms. The rooms are modern. The owner is friendly. The rooms are cleaned and made every day.

voyage.name: New Fortunate Guesthouse, International Inn
voyage.content: One of the nicer guesthouses in the building. Rooms are small but clean and cheerful. A double room with A/C, TV and in-room wireless internet access should cost around $250 per night, perhaps less during low quieter times or for those willing to bargain hard.

voyage.name: Travellers Hostel
voyage.address: Flat A1 & A2, Block A, 16/F, Chungking Mansions
voyage.content: A long-established and with a reasonable reputation.

voyage.name: Welcome Guest House
voyage.address: A Block, 7th floor, Room 5, Chungking Mansions
voyage.content: Good guest house: doubles go for $180, are fairly roomy and are equipped with AC, fridge, TV, telephone and bathrooms with hot shower and toilet. Singles are $130, are positively tiny and don't have a fridge. Most rooms, apart from those farthest from the reception, have free Wi-Fi. Rooms are clean but mediocre (leaky sinks, some cracked tiles, nothing too serious); sheets are changed and rooms cleaned daily. The big

voyage.name: Whole Sunshine Hotel
voyage.content: They also own 4th floor but it is being refurbished. Feels like a junior manager's love nest, with circular bed (very firm) and hourly rates. Welcoming, manager has enough English, clean, small room, a/c works but seldom hot water. No room safe.

voyage.name: Cosmic Guest House
voyage.content: A clean hostel with mostly friendly staff, you can get clean dorms here. or bargain for a good deal on one of the tiny private rooms with air-conditioning and cable TV.

voyage.name: Garden Hostel
voyage.content: Long-established place, dorm beds with hot water bathrooms. Has a garden to sit in.

voyage.name: USA Hostel Hong Kong
voyage.content: Located in an old building that is also home to stores and other commercial enterprises, expect a budget hotel which (usually) is clean. Ask to see the room first, or you'll get a really small one. Generally, the next day they will move you out of the good room into one of the smaller ones. Also don't be surprised to see the television and shower not function properly.

voyage.name: Dragon Hostel
voyage.content: Tiny but clean rooms with aircon and free Internet at reception. Located on the 7th floor and a short walking distance from Mong Kok MTR Station.

voyage.name: Hakkas Guest House
voyage.address: Flat l 3/f., 13-15 Jordan Rd, Yau Ma Tei
voyage.content: This well-maintained guesthouse is home to 10 immaculate rooms and is one of the best budget deals at the Yau Ma Tei end of Nathan Rd.

voyage.name: Hop Inn
voyage.content: A clean and stylish hostel with friendly staff, one of the best in the Tsim Sha Tsui area. Each room was designed by a different local artist/illustrator (very interesting). They also have another nearby location at 5/F, Lyton Building, 36 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui

voyage.name: Lee Garden Guest House
voyage.content: Tiny but clean rooms, this hostel is in a great location, near the MTR station and a few blocks from Nathan Road.

voyage.name: YHA Mei Ho House Youth Hostel
voyage.content: YHA hostel in the Mei Ho House, the last remaining example of a "Mark I" building (historic H-shaped public housing block), formerly part of Shek Kip Mei Estate (the first public housing estate in Hong Kong) and also the base of the rioters during Hong Kong 1956 riots. You can either stay in a modern room or a 1970s themed one. The dormitories are all modern. There is also a museum about early public housing (open Tu

voyage.name: Rainbow Lodge HK
voyage.address: Flat 501, 5/F, Hai Phong Mansion, 101 Nathan Road
voyage.content: Clean, convenient, and well-designed hostel on Nathan Road in Tsim Sha Tsui with big lockers, good wifi, air conditioning, and curtains on the bunks. The common area is small but lively, with a refrigerator and microwave. It's in a touristy area, which has both benefits and drawbacks: avoid the restaurants in the immediate area, which seem to be priced out of proportion with their quality.

voyage.name: Chelsea Hotel
voyage.price: $700 for single occupancy in double room
voyage.address: Hanoi Road, corner of Mody Rd
voyage.content: Quite a bit nicer than the budget places, not a lot more expensive, prime location.

voyage.name: Eaton Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.content: Hotel overlooking Nathan Rd.

voyage.name: Harbour Plaza Metropolis
voyage.content: Rooms overlooking the harbour. Large outdoor swimming pool.

voyage.name: The Salisbury YMCA
voyage.content: Hong Kong's main YMCA and a well regarded hotel. All rooms have private bathrooms and some have good views of the harbour. The location, next to the Peninsula Hotel and near the Tsim Sha Tsui MTR station, can't be beaten. Popular with budget-minded families. Reservations well in advance are highly recommended. Other Y services (swimming pool, gym, restaurants, etc.) are available to hotel guests either free or at rea

voyage.name: Dorsett Mongkok Hotel
voyage.content: Provides free use of smart phone with free 4G Internet with IDD facilities to 9 countries, Wi-Fi, mosaic bathroom with massage shower and rain shower head.

voyage.name: The Cityview
voyage.content: Run by the Chinese YMCA, the former YMCA International House.

voyage.name: Park Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.address: 61 – 65 Chatham Road South, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: Refurbished in 2020, and rooms have the amenities one can expect from an upper mid-range hotel in a first-world country. There's a cafe and a bar.

voyage.name: Regal Oriental Hotel
voyage.content: Originally named "Regal Meridien Hong Kong Airport Hotel" and built as the airport hotel for the old Kai Tak Airport, with a footbridge connecting it to the terminal building. The footbridge and terminal building have since been demolished after the airport was closed down in 1998, but the hotel remains standing.

voyage.name: Hyatt Regency Hong Kong, Tsim Sha Tsui
voyage.content: 381 rooms and suites with views of the harbour and Kowloon skyline, Sky Garden and outdoor pool. Guestroom amenities: work area, marble bath, Wi-Fi. Regency Club Lounge for free continental breakfast, private concierge and secretarial services.

voyage.name: Regent Hong Kong
voyage.content: On the waterfront, good views of the harbour and the Hong Kong skyline.

voyage.name: Kowloon Shangri-La
voyage.address: 64 Mody Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui East

voyage.name: Langham Hotel Hong Kong
voyage.content: An elegant European-style hotel.

voyage.name: Cordis Hong Kong
voyage.content: Hotel built in 2004. Adjacent to a modern shopping mall.

voyage.name: Peninsula Hong Kong
voyage.content: Hong Kong's grand old historic hotel has a commanding presence with some of Hong Kong's best bars, restaurants and luxury boutiques (and equally commanding prices starting at around $2,500 per night). Or how about the $50,000 honeymoon suite package including a helicopter tour of the city? The hotel was the venue where British governor Mark Young surrendered to the Japanese and was taken over as a military headquarte

voyage.name: Regal Kowloon Hotel
voyage.content: 600 rooms and suites with Wi-Fi.

voyage.name: Red House
voyage.address: Near Lung Mun Road, Tuen Mun. In the park. Near TM Public Riding School.
voyage.content: This is a memorial building to Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The house and the farm was where Dr. Sun Yat-sen planned to overthrow the Qing dynasty. It is named after its appearance, red bricks with plastering in red. The two-storey house is a combination of Chinese and Western architecture. Adjacent to the house is a garden commemorating Dr. Sun Yat Sen and is one of a few places in Hong Kong where the Flag of the Republic of Ch

voyage.name: Ping Shan Heritage Trail
voyage.content: This is a kilometre long trail enabling you to take in the most important buildings in this historical area, including the ancient pagoda of Tsui Sing Lau, the Tang Ancestral Hall and the Kun Ting Study Hall.

voyage.name: Tsang Tai Uk
voyage.alt: 曾大屋; lit. Big House of the Tsangs

voyage.name: Maclehose Trail
voyage.content: Stage I is ~3 hours, stage II ~6 hours of walking for a total of 10 stages and 100km. Parts are sealed/concrete road, other parts dirt/rock. if you hike late, take a light as public lights are sparse. Altitude is between 0 and 300m (Sai Wan Shan). Camping sites are available.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Wetland Park
voyage.content: Is a relaxing park set amidst an ecological mitigation area. One can stroll along a network of board walks built over the marshy area and watch birds from a tower. The park also features a large visitors centre/museum. The museum has many interactive exhibits ideal for children, as well as some live animal habitats. To visit, take MTR West Rail to Tin Shui Wai Station, then the #705 light rail to Wetland Park. The pa

voyage.name: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark
voyage.content: Different rock formations and geological features are found here.The park is an area of 150 km2 across parts of the eastern and northeastern New Territories.

voyage.name: Tai Mo Shan
voyage.content: The highest point in Hong Kong, at about 956 m above sea level or 957 m above the Hong Kong Principal Datum. You hike almost to the summit, but not all the way as the summit houses a weather station and military outpost.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Heritage Museum
voyage.hours: Mon Wed-Fri 10AM-6PM, Sat Sun 10AM-7PM (closed Tue plus first ane second day of Chinese New Year)
voyage.content: For those with a serious interest in Chinese culture, this might appeal to you as one of Hong Kong's best museums. Modern, informative and attractively presented, this museum houses several permanent exhibitions of life in the New Territories, Cantonese opera, and Chinese art, as well as temporary exhibitions of a high calibre.

voyage.name: Hong Kong Railway Museum
voyage.hours: Open from 10AM-6PM on Mon and Wed-Sunday. Closing is 1 hour earlier (5PM) on Christmas Eve and Lunar New Year's Eve. Closed on Tuesdays (except public holidays) and first two days of Lunar New Year.
voyage.address: 13 Shung Tak Street, Tai Po Market, Tai Po
voyage.content: An open-air museum converted from the old Tai Po Railway Station. It has seven railway coaches and two locomotives.

voyage.name: Jockey Club Museum of Climate Change
voyage.hours: Mon Tue Thu-Sat 09:30-17:00. Closed on Wednesdays, Sundays, public holidays and university holidays (including Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve)
voyage.address: Yasumoto International Academic Park, 8th Floor, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin

voyage.name: The Art Museum, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
voyage.address: Art Museum, Institute of Chinese Studies, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Sha Tin
voyage.content: M-W F Sa from 10AM-5PM, Sunday and public holidays from 1:00-5PM, closed Th (except public holidays), New Year, Lunar New Year, Easter, and Christmas holidays. Admission is free.

voyage.name: Tao Heung Museum of Food Culture
voyage.hours: Tours Sat Sun holidays from 9:30AM to 5:15PM
voyage.address: 13 Au Pui Wan St, Fo Tan
voyage.content: Museum displays cooking utensils, cutlery, spices from different time periods around the world and the food culture of Hong Kong. Advance online reservation is required. Each session lasts 75 minutes. Guide will narrate in Cantonese for 45 minutes followed by 30 minutes of free tour.

voyage.name: Tsz Shan Monastery Buddhist Art Museum
voyage.alt: 慈山寺佛教藝術博物館
voyage.hours: 10:00-13:00 (last admission at 12:30), 14:00-17:00 (last admission at 16:30), closed on Mondays (except Mondays that fall on a public holiday)
voyage.address: No. 88, Universal Gate Road, Tai Po

voyage.name: Sam Tung Uk Museum
voyage.content: A Hakka walled-village that was built in 1786.

voyage.name: Sha Tau Kok Anti-Japanese War Memorial Hall
voyage.address: 39 Sha Tau Kok Road (Shek Chung Au), Sha Tau Kok
voyage.content: Opened in September 2022, this is the first comprehensive museum about the Second World War in Hong Kong. The museum is at the former home of the Luo Family, which was the first base of operations for Communist-led guerrilla fighters from the Mainland who came across the border to help resist the Japanese. At the present time, the museum is only accepting group visits and bookings are essential. As the museum is outs

voyage.name: Castle Peak Monastery
voyage.content: Classed as a Grade I historic building that has been standing for more than 1000 years. These historic monuments have stood through the ages in a tranquil woodland area. The striking and picturesque surroundings create an enjoyable view, as well as a solemn ambiance. Upon entering the monastery, you will notice the words "香海名山" (Fragrant Sea and Prestigious Mountain) engraved on the portico. The Tsing Shan Temple is

voyage.name: 10,000 Buddhas Monastery
voyage.content: This rather garish but enjoyable modern temple dating from the 1950s in fact contains no less than 12,800 Buddhas lining the walls of the main hall. There's also a nine-story pagoda and some smaller temples above the main complex. Half the fun is getting there, the 500-metre path that climbs up the hill is lined with life-sized golden plastic statues of Buddhas in poses ranging from serene to outrageous. A point of m

voyage.name: Miu Fat Buddhist Monastery
voyage.content: This is a temple built in 1960 and is one of the best monasteries for visitors to enjoy.

voyage.name: Ching Chung Koon
voyage.content: A traditional Taoist temple. Many people go to here to worship the gods.

voyage.name: Kat Hing Wai
voyage.content: Of more historical than practical interest, this tiny walled village was one of the first settlements of the Tang clan, who arrived in Hong Kong in the 12th century and have dominated much of the area ever since. The village today, however, has lots of nondescript modern low-rise concrete housing blocks crammed behind a crumbling gray brick wall. $1 donation requested, and if you see the old Hakka women lounging near

voyage.name: Lam Tsuen Wishing Tree
voyage.content: The Wishing Tree is an old tree. Traditionally, it is believed that it will bring good luck and fortune. Nowadays, it is a tourist spot for both Westerners and locals. Simply go to Tai Po Market Railway Station and take the green minibus route 25K, or bus 64K to get to the Wishing Tree. Alternatively, you are advised to take a green taxi from Tai Wo Railway Station if you have 4 or 5 people travelling together.

voyage.name: Man Mo Temple
voyage.content: A temple built in the 1890s, it is regarded by many as a must-see tourist destination in Hong Kong.

voyage.name: Sha Tin Racecourse
voyage.content: Participate in the most popular sport in Hong Kong at games held most Saturday afternoons from September to June. Regular stand seats $10, but a special package available to overseas tourists-only allows box access for $130-190.

voyage.name: Jockey Club Kau Sai Chau Public Golf Course
voyage.content: Hong Kong's only public golf course, comprising three 18-hole courses. Accessible by ferry from Sai Kung.

voyage.name: Tai Po Waterfront Park
voyage.content: The Tai Po Waterfront Park is the largest park in Tai Po District. The Park provides a wide range of facilities including a 1.2 long promenade, rest-gardens, sitting-out areas, a jogging trail with fitness stations, a cycling track and a 600-seat amphitheatre. There is also a 32.4-metre-high Lookout Tower in the Park. After visiting the tower, visitors may move on to the Insect House nearby. Take a green taxi instead

voyage.name: Tai Mei Tuk
voyage.content: Tai Mei Tuk is famous for the natural view of Pat Sin Leng and Plover Cove Reservoir, the largest reservoir in Hong Kong. You can also make use of the free barbecue site in Tai Mei Tuk and the adjoining country park. Get off from Tai Po Market Railway Station and take bus 75K or green minibus 20C.

voyage.name: Kam Shan Country Park
